Respiratory metabolism in the Black-streaked puffbird (Malacoptila fulvogularis) has been investigated under controlled laboratory conditions that closely mimic the thermal environment of its natural habitat. During active metabolic periods, individuals measured at a body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C] exhibited a basal oxygen consumption rate of 96.36 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 96.36 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic value, corresponding to maximum resting metabolism, provides a benchmark for understanding the energetic costs of thermoregulation in a mid-elevation forest species. The incubation of eggs at a distinct thermal regime of 39 °C [T = 39 °C] yields an incubation period, or age at hatching, of 14 days [ab = 14 days], a timing that aligns closely with durations reported for its relative Micromonacha lanceolata. Newly hatched nestlings emerge at a wet weight of 8.8 grams [Ww0 = 8.8 grams], a modest initial mass that suggests a significant energetic commitment to postnatal growth is required before the chick can achieve thermal independence.

A comprehensive field study on a marked population in the eastern Andes allowed for the reconstruction of key life-history milestones under the prevailing thermal conditions of the breeding season. Under an ambient regime equivalent to an internal body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], the rapid developmental phase leading to fledging was observed to be completed in 22.5 days since birth [tx = 22.5 days since birth], a relatively brief nestling period that is typical of many puffbird species. Following this, the onset of gonadal maturation—representing the time since birth at puberty—was recorded at 67.5 days since birth [tp = 67.5 days since birth] when measured at the same body temperature at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This interval marks the transition to a physiologically mature juvenile capable of future reproductive investment. The coordinate timing of these events suggests a tightly scheduled developmental program that maximizes the use of the seasonal food pulse.

Reproductive output in the Black-streaked puffbird reflects a strategy of high parental investment per breeding attempt. Adult females produce one to two eggs per clutch, and annual reproductive frequency is limited. Data from monitored nests indicate that females lay one to two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = one to two eggs per clutch], with a single successful clutch being the norm each year [F_R_i = single successful clutch being the norm each year]. The first successful breeding event is deferred until approximately 511 days since birth [tR = approximately 511 days since birth], a delay that allows for complete somatic growth and the establishment at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]of a territory. This extended prereproductive period, measured at the typical adult body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], is consistent with the relatively slow-paced life history observed in related bucconids. The production of a single annual brood likely constrains the species' ability to recover from population perturbations.

Body size dimorphism is apparent in this species, with adult females attaining a greater ultimate wet weight than males. Based on measurements from a series of museum specimens and live captures, the maximum adult body mass recorded for females is 57.4 grams [Wwi = 57.4 grams], which falls slightly below the upper bound of 65.0 grams suggested by earlier anecdotal accounts. This female-biased size difference is a common pattern among puffbirds and is thought to be related to the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. Longevity data from band returns and captive records indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 3577 days [am = approximately 3577 days] when individuals are maintained under a stable thermal regime of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. Such a lifespan, spanning nearly a decade, is considerable for a bird of this body size and implies a low rate of extrinsic mortality in its montane forest environment.

The ecological context of the Black-streaked puffbird's life history becomes clearer when its developmental timing is viewed alongside its metabolic requirements. The rapid progression from a neonatal mass of 8.8 grams [Ww0 = 8.8 grams] to the adult female mass of 57.4 grams [Wwi = 57.4 grams] requires a substantial and consistent food supply during the nestling and fledgling phases. The probability of achieving a first successful reproduction event at 511 days since birth [tR = 511 days since birth] is likely influenced by habitat quality and territory availability at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. Furthermore, the maximum recorded longevity of 3577 days [am = 3577 days] suggests that adults, once established, may enjoy high survival rates at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. The species' reliance on a single annual clutch [F_R_i = single annual clutch] and a clutch size of one to two eggs [N_R_i = a clutch size of one to two eggs] positions it as a K-selected strategist, vulnerable to any environmental change that disrupts adult survival or the brief window for successful fledging within the 22.5 day [tx = 22.5 day] period since birth at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C].
